50379221.text:
Hey everyone! @mozgiii and I have been working on Waymark for the better part of the last year. Waymark’s an open source durable execution library with similar functionality to Temporal or DBOS.

I fell in love with durable execution a few years ago, after working at a company with a heavy pubsub architecture. In comparison to job orchestrators that force a certain task design or special syntax, many of these durable libs lets you write business logic in regular code: `asyncio.gather` to parallelize tasks, `for` loops, conditionals, and let the runtime figure out how to run them efficiently across a cluster of nodes. But most of the current solutions require a heavy broker, runtime hacks to try to ensure deterministic workflow logic, and feel like you have to learn a whole new ecosystem just to get started.

A few unique design decisions in waymark:

— Write jobs in normal code (right now Python but JS coming soon). Instead of running control flow as-is, which requires booting up an interpreter to replay past state, we’ll just compile your code directly. We walk your AST and map your logic to our stackless VM bytecode. We support variables, conditionals, await, sleep, helper functions, loops... basically what you’d expect in workflow logic.

— Since we’re compiling a language subset, we can proactively flag errors in your workflows locally instead of when they run in production.

— It only requires Postgres as the task broker. We’ve spent a lot of time tuning our design to play nicely with its strengths and limitations; our current benchmarks show around 1500 workflows/second but we still have some more optimization work to do here.

— Actions plug-and-play with FastAPI’s dependency injection syntax. So if you already have an ecosystem based on typehinting/DI, it should fit like a glove.

It allows for parallelization of workflows across one machine or a whole cluster. The bulk of the work per node is done by our central Rust core - which distributes workflows to properly saturate all cores. The idea is to be as batteries included as possible with the broker, webapp, and runtime.

What to use it for? It works great as the runner loop controlling agents, but it also works well for basically any task that you need to kick off in the background. It’s largely replaced our way of writing api code. Most frontend actions at this point just push to a simple REST endpoint that kick off a background job.

I spent an embarrassing amount of time making our https://waymark.sh site interactive - it’s probably the best place to learn more. We’re starting with Python support and looking for community input on what language to ship next. Would love to hear your thoughts!

Norvig (and Chomsky) are talking at cross purposes.

Norvig confuses engineering for science. If an engineer wants something that works (and guarantees that it will work) then you use the most effective tool available to achieve that goal. No problem there. But there's absolutely no reason to think that tells you anything scientific about the phenomenon you're modeling. For example, aeronautical engineering says very little about how birds fly. And - currently relevant - LLMs learn to use and understand language, but they use millions of times more training data, and millions of times more computing power, than a child does. So an LLM may be a great technology, but it's probably not a good model for how humans learn and use language.

Chomsky OTOH doesn't see any use for statistics in science, at least not in linguistics. Fortunately for the field of linguistics, Chomsky's influence in linguistics is waning and linguists are beginning to use statistical tools to do science.

50392663.text:
> Turboprop engines tell us nothing about how birds fly

That is not true.

Turboprop engines and flying birds are different things, but there is a set of common properties.

A blade of a screw propeller functions exactly in the same way as a flapping wing of a bird, except that the wing cannot rotate without limits around the body of the bird, so it must stop, change angles and revert the motion, while the blade can rotate continuously around the axis, functioning on one side like a falling wing and on the other side like a raising wing. The similarities between propeller blades and insect wings are even greater, because insect wings cannot change their shapes so much as those of birds.

For now, our understanding of the networks composed of the neurons of animals is much less advanced than our understanding of wings and propellers, which is why there is a much greater uncertainty about whether there are any similar mechanisms in biological neural networks and in LLMs.

My objection is "simpler." What's so "simple" about a probabilistic model? It takes an enormous amount of calculations, so much that you have to predigest incoming information into high-level chunks in order to have any chance of calculating it over small inputs with reasonable effort.

A probabilistic model is the most complicated model. It doesn't even attempt to model the problem, it just looks at the results of an enormous number of tries with different inputs, goes through them all, finds the most similar cases to the current input, and blends them together in a way that carefully avoids any self-contradictory or absurd result.

We see this plainly with LLMs. You train an LLM on a thousand times the (high-level, pre-digested) input that the average human has gotten, and the average human thinks it's a hallucinating moron. It doesn't start to converge on something that passes the smell test to you average human idiot until it has been trained on a million times the input the average human has gotten.

It's not doing what a human does, it's guessing what a human (or any system) might do when confronted with X input. They're not even similar activities, even if they have identical output in the limit. It's like confusing gravity for equations about gravity. Being able to make perfect predictions about the positions of moving, nearby frictionless spherical things in a vacuum at time t doesn't tell us a thing about what gravity is. It tells us how it looks. It should, we distilled it by watching things for a very long time.

> Is a probabilistic model not the only model able to deal with uncertainty?

No, all models deal with uncertainty. The entire point of a model is that it is what you know about a system when you don't know its inputs. The variables in a model are uncertainty. The model is dealing with it.

edit: I think you're interpreting "uncertainty" as a numerical probability. A numerical probability is an artifact of the set of data you're calculating it from, not a thing with independent existence. "Uncertainty" is just a thing that you don't know yet.

If you assume that "uncertainty" is a knowable numeric probability that contributes to some calculation, you're begging the question when you say that the only way you can model it is through probabilistic calculations.

I don't think it's the simplest, actually. Off the top of my mind:

Ternary logic is a super simple model; where true AND unknown equals unknown, and true OR unknown equals true. This deals with uncertainty and ambiguity, just not the probability; notionally you could say everything is 50-50.

Same thing if you have e.g. text-to-speech which returns "the b??? dog" rather than "the (0.8:black, 0.1:blue, 0.1:boy) dog" - no probabilities. Of course, maybe later in the processing you add probabilities back in.

Then there's fuzzy logic, which uses scores that are typically numbers, but those don't express actual probabilities, but more like vibes. They don't necessarily add up to 1, for instance, and you don't apply Bayes' formula to them, or even multiply them, you can use addition too - yolo.

Edit: and also of course backtracking, beam search, that sort of stuff - needn't use probabilities, just heuristics.

50394202.text:
I've worked on systems this decade that still relied on floppy disks. It's getting harder and harder for them to operate because the disks are getting rarer, as are the drives. And often the essential component is not the disk itself. There are some other computers in the system that cannot be upgraded to any more recent device, systems from the 1980s and 1990s that force them to continue using a floppy disk.

If it was just two modern computers and transferring data between them, the floppy disk would have been dropped in a heartbeat. But it's the old computers still in the critical path that are holding everything back. And those are really hard to maintain. Last year we phased out a system that was dependent on computers from the mid-1990s, getting replacement parts was practically impossible, they mostly just don't exist. You'd buy old systems off ebay and hope that they had enough working parts to scavenge, and the right working parts.

EDIT: Light editing because I had some extra words.

50394894.text:
It's more or less the classic clash of two modernist attitudes, that of the rationalist (Chomsky) and the empiricist (Norvig). The intellectual wound this division introduces is longstanding. However, I would say Norvig has the overall advantage.

1. Norvig is correct that observation and fact/data collection are necessary for science. However, Chomsky is correct that the ultimate goal of science is to determine the principles governing something. Ergo: you need the first to do the second. The intellect abstracts from source data, but nothing is in the intellect that is not first in the senses.

2. Chomsky here is uninterested in things like speech - he only cares about the underlying syntax. But syntax - expressed and instantiated in matter - is known through speech, and probabilities presuppose an underlying determinate syntax. Ergo: a complete science of speech is end-to-end, from the "reading" or interpretation of noisy data through syntactic processing all the way through to expression.

3. Chomsky focuses heavily on internal generation. Norvig points out that interpretation is a separate, highly practical challenge. Figuring out what someone means in a noisy, ambiguous world is an exercise in prudence which involves weighing contingencies and probabilities to arrive at the most likely truth. Of course, this can only be done against a presupposed acceptance of the function of speech which is to communicate meaning and what is true (hence why lies work and why they are an abuse of speech). Probabilistic reasoning is still reasoning. It's reasoning in the face of incomplete information (against a backdrop of presuppositions) which is a component of prudential reasoning.

To me uncertainty on a given quantity, is represented by a probability distribution function giving how probable the value of a given quantity is. Loosely, it can also be represented by a confidence interval. It is not intrinsic to the quantity, but how much we know about this quantity.

For the domain I am working in, a model is considered deterministic if for a set of input it always provide the same output and the input are assumed to be perfectly known. A model become probabilistic, once the input or the model itself are considered as uncertain. As an example: previously weather models always provided singe prediction for tomorrow, for example rain or no rain. But now, such models are probabilistic in the sense that an ensemble of model forecast are made (with slightly different input representing our uncertainties) to provide an estimate of the probabilities. Indeed such probabilistic model is not the simplest, but to most complete and so far the only practical way to handle with uncertainty for system like the weather as far as I am aware of.

50396658.text:
> Which is why many systems on most airliners are redundant in threes

Not really. Triplex redundancy is based on a failure model where failures can produce arbitrary output. Three systems allows majority voting (often, median select) to provide correct output in the presence of a single arbitrary failure. It allows detection of double-fail-silent failures and uncorrelated double failures, but that's not really the point, since continued operation under these conditions is at risk, and failing nonoperational isn't often acceptable for these systems. (You'll also see quadruplex systems that use the same voting mechanism to detect and disable failed channels, allowing handling two arbitrary non-simultaneous failures, for systems that need a longer window of continued operation after failure.)

If you change the failure modes, you change the architecture. These days you often see dual-dual systems where each pair of systems cross-checks and disables itself on mismatch, converting a single arbitrary failure to a single silent failure; which then allows downstream systems to accept inputs from two such fail-silent systems and trust either that is providing output, removing the need for a median select.

50396963.text:
(Although this comment discusses an AI-written project, the comment itself is entirely human-written.)

It's probably worth pointing out that, unless you're writing a replacement for GRUB, Multiboot2 is a reasonable alternative to building a UEFI PE32+ image, and it permits you to still call UEFI services: https://www.gnu.org/software/grub/manual/multiboot2/multiboo... https://wiki.osdev.org/Multiboot

I was pleased last week that I could elicit enough of a UEFI environment from Opus 5.5 to be able to build an UEFI application without enormous, un-auditable dependencies like gnu-efi. Claude distilled the relevant parts of the UEFI interface into a 289-line header file. The example application just displays the keyboard and mouse events on a UEFI framebuffer using a vendored pixel font, thus the name "inputmon": http://canonical.org/~kragen/sw/inputmon-3.tar.gz

The Makefile includes a "run" target to boot it under QEMU with the OVMF implementation of UEFI.

(One fairly surprising feature of all this is that, not counting the time Claude was waiting for me, it took the model a total of about 7 minutes to write and test this. These 7 minutes were spread over almost 15 hours because I ran out of tokens and spent time thinking. This might be a good example of a case where an LLM is literally a million times more productive than a human programmer: the task is algorithmically trivial, and it doesn't involve difficult engineering tradeoffs, but involves deep knowledge of a pile of obfuscated recondite interfaces that are publicly documented and widely used by published open-source software. It is something I've wanted to do for 7 million minutes.)

I'm hoping I can get an in-browser demo of inputmon working next week, but that's probably going to involve doing some surgery on Bochs in order to get an amd64-compatible virtual machine that doesn't require multithreading the way QEMU does.

Inputmon does have the enormous, un-auditable dependency of LLVM and Clang, but that's a horror I'm already resigned to. But with clang, lld, and make, you can build the image from source, and with QEMU and OVMF you can run it in a virtual machine.

I think it's a little bit debatable to call UEFI "bare metal" (Boone responds: "this is a fair criticism"), and I'm particularly skeptical of Boone's claim that you can guarantee microsecond response times in the face of SMM, but whatever.

I think you just explained the situation, even if you didn't realize it.

LLMs process millions of times more text data and use millions of times more compute power to learn a language, mostly because we know how to do that technologically.

Children use much less text data, but also use a lot of other kinds of data, including interacting with other humans, to learn language. We have no idea how that works. And, on top of that, people can interact with pets of various species in the same way as children, but those pets never learn language.

The actual vulnerability got very little discussion. It's clever. Because Linux networking people are obsessed with checksum performance, virtio-net plumbs checksum offload metadata through the host/guest driver interface. Guests can thus deliver the host packets along with instructions on what to checksum. The vulnerability is a missing sanity check that allows checksum instructions to instruct the host to overwrite the header length field in the IPv4 header, rather than the checksum field.

Crucially, this happens in the middle of packet processing, so the kernel code is forced to work with two different ideas of how long the IPv4 header is. All hell predictably breaks loose.

> the formally-verified configuration of seL4 doesn't actually do much

As a systems security engineer myself I would disagree and know several others that would as well. All depends on your circles, applications, and threat model I suppose.

Xen, Hyper-V, and KVM have all had major security flaws in the form of logic violations, spacial memory corruptions, use-after-free, and pointer corruptions that allowed hypervisor trust boundary violations. I expect most if not all of those classes of bugs could have been prevented by formal verification.

Xen likely has a bad reputation with both of us because of a history of preventable flaws like these.

In my applications every single daemon gets its own sandbox, which is a VM whenever possible. Some with network, some without network, different filesystem and vsock access for maximum damage control and minimal trust between daemons. The hypervisor is the most important security boundary to me especially when isolating user-controlled workloads. The more confidence I can get that it is correct the better.

Counterarguments to that premise:

1. Intelligence per dollar spent/token output seems to be increasing rapidly. Opus 4 was $15/75 per million input/output tokens when released. Opus 5.5, which is significantly better, is $4/15. Sure it cost more money upfront to train Opus 5.5, or the bigger model (Fable 5.5) which tuned it, but once it is reached, there are massive diffusive effects.

2. The capital equation is still favoring more spend. Anthropic's revenue is growing rapidly and they are profitable on inference. Huge upfront spend for realized gains later on is standard for R&D. As long as serving the models is profitable and generates more value than the energy/compute consumed

3. The search space is too large to assume that improvement in AI assisted research is just models dumbly trying every combination until something works. For every additional bit searched, the space doubles, so even a trivially small combinatorial exploration incurs prohibitively large costs. Intelligent searching which continuously prunes that space along dimensions of effectiveness is not a trivial skill and is among the emergent accoutrements of these smarter models.

50399881.text:
> Norvig confuses engineering for science

I don’t think Norvig is confused. He explicitly addresses this point right at the top of the article.

His argument is that successfully engineering a system using a statistical method provides some bits of evidence for the hypothesis that the system itself is statistical.

Which is obviously true, so long as we take care to weigh evidence properly.

> there's absolutely no reason to think that tells you anything scientific about the phenomenon you're modeling

No, this is not how evidence works. If you can accurately model a system with method X and you cannot come up with a model that works with method Y, you should think it’s more likely (but not certain) that X is the actual physical model.

And indeed modern cognitive science (see Predictive Processing) also has a bunch of evidence for the brain as a hierarchical predictor, rather than a rule engine.

To your points - planes are not model organisms of birds, but they do shed insight on the bounds that birds must obey, eg thrust-to-weight etc. And the sample efficiency point really needs to die. The human brain is born with an extremely complex prior baked in. An LLM begins pretraining with almost nothing (just a very simple architecture and a few simple algorithms like attention), and has to learn the basic architecture of cognition from scratch. A better baseline would be how many samples were processed by every animal in our genetic ancestry that had a brain, since brains existed.

50400223.text:
Yep, that’s exactly it. imo the main value add for agents:

- Each LLM call and tool call becomes a checkpoint. Without durable execution you're pretty much stuck doing db saves/restores if you detect that this agent might have a previous context window. Agent frameworks are fundamentally just harnesses around the underlying model: you `while loop` until some server gives you some payload back, you add that to your context window list, and you keep going until it terminates. Durable execution moves that loop into the workflow body itself (a quick example here https://www.waymark.sh/python/tutorials/building-a-from-scra...).

- Long waits. Sometimes you do want your agent to wait for an arbitrary amount of time (ie. wait for this compilation job to finish - look again in 5mins, or maybe 5 hours). Durable execution makes sure that sleep timer will wake up regardless of what happens in the system state.

- Easier monitorability. Instead of having to sift through interleaved logs to figure out what was going on, you can see every large function call with a clean input/output contract. Useful especially in tracing down raised Exceptions and the data flow that it took to get there. Good for agents and regular code alike.

Of course, if your system is largely idempotent or your agents are mostly classifiers that are working in short internals - a simple db save/restore can work perfectly well too.

50400468.text:
Every dot in these graphs is composed of multiple benchmarks smooshed together.

Benchmarks are by definition a curated set of things that can be measured and evaluated.

Things that can be measured and evaluated can be (expensively) trained on.

The progress we are observing comes from figuring out how to measure and evaluate particular aspects of intelligence, and then expensively training on feedback loops made of those exact measurements, and synthesized data representing further measurements (literally benchmaxing).

What is not shown in these graphs are the set of things that intelligence can do, which are difficult, expensive or impossible to measure and evaluate.

That set of things is much larger than the set of benchmarks represented in the graph.

Therefore the post is misleading in the sense that the "superintelligence" being targeted is "jagged" to use Karpathy's term, and we infact already have jagged superintelligence (calculators, compilers, Bayesian spam classifiers, etc.)

We are witnessing a profound explosion of much more jagged superintelligence, restricted to the exact domains that can be (expensively) RL'ed on.

50400602.text:
Every time I'm in a place of business with shiny computers, I'm reminded of the difference in efficiency between the newest systems and the 'green screen' terminals and other similar tech that was everywhere in 1990.

Most of those were extremely optimized for their specific purposes - for instance, screens were carefully designed to fit all the necessary information to complete a task without any scrolling. They had extremely low latency despite all the hardware being potato-grade compared to what we have today.

When latency existed, simple things like the keyboard buffer allowed the skilled user to get ahead of the machine and move onto another task, while the processing caught up.

Today, it's all a webapp with a ton of React, probably 5,000 npm modules, and you get to watch skeletal loading rectangles pulsating after every click (or branded animations on the "customer-facing" flavor). Instead of having muscle memory of hands on a keyboard (usually a specialized one which gave a dedicated key to every important function), the user must move their arm to find touch targets placed at arbitrary places across a 24" touchscreen, and often hunting for functions inside ••• menus.

Obviously, no usability testing has been done on any of these. Or if it has, the only thing tested was "Can a 17-year-old with zero skills ploddingly complete a transaction (the happy path only!), after only 15 minutes of training?"

So yeah, I never listen to any "newer = better" takes.

50400611.text:
Well, it was just that the models didn't really line up.

To give a somewhat longer description of what Pachyderm does/did:

1. Connect data-scale version control with pipeline orchestrator.

2. Version control tells orchestrator which shards have changed since the last run and which ones haven't.

3. Orchestrator only processes changed shards from one run to the next, instead of all of them.

4. Profit.

That's fine for e.g. one mapreduce, but,

1. If an action's behavior changes, you can't re-use its prior results (usually—sometimes you're just adding print statements to debug a failing shard)

2. If the overall pipeline changes, you can't re-use results from the first change onward

3. Figuring out if the overall pipeline changed is not necessarily easy, and if you're always throwing out everything just in case, your product is not helping people.

So, the way Waymark uses a compiler for the orchestration layer would've worked so well with our model.

It's also just satisfying—once I learned in detail how Bazel/Nix work, I see a fit for that architecture pattern in anything remotely pipeline-y, and it drove me nuts that Airflow/Beam/Dataflow weren't really using it. So I'm very happy to see this for that reason as well. And, as if that weren't enough, it's so cool that it introduces a pure language at the coordination layer (which this type of architecture basically needs, hence the Nix language/Starlark) without actually requiring a new language, or even a new file. Amazing!

I believe this conclusion is flawed. The author argues:

1) Unitree robots are largely made by hand.

2) Labor is approximately 8% of cost of manufacturing these robots. Because these costs are not prohibitive, there is little incentive to automate.

3) Labor costs are higher in America.

4) Therefore, American companies have higher incentive to automate.

5) Therefore, the West will capture most of the robotics opportunity.

Arguments 1-4 are reasonable, but 5 is a non-sequitur. Higher incentive to automate does not imply a better ability to automate & scale manufacturing.

I believe Unitree is currently assembling robots by hand for practical reasons:

1) Labor is still relatively cheap.

2) Humanoids and robots are evolving rapidly, changing every few months.

3) Custom assembly lines are expensive, and become obsolete when the product changes. It's difficult to maintain an assembly line when the product is rapidly evolving.

4) Tooling is inadequate. Some robotic parts are delicate, complicated, and difficult to automate manufacturing of. American companies have hit the exact same problem: Tesla is assembling the hand/forearm of Optimus by hand because it hasn't figured out how to automate manufacturing them. https://www.theverge.com/tech/1016492/tesla-optimus-robots-p... . Apparently, Tesla has hundreds of handless Optimus robots just standing around, waiting for hand manufacturing to catch up.

5) Demand is still relatively niche, these are not mass market products. Unitree only sold 5,500 robots last year. There is not enough demand to justify massive automated lines.

The author also ignores the biggest counterpoint: the Chinese have already demonstrated mastery in automated manufacturing, and have proven they can run dark factories (factories without humans) at a better scale than the west.

When humanoid robots become a mass market product (they are not ready today because the software side is majorly lacking), Chinese manufacturers are in an excellent position to rapidly automate.

As somebody who does ML research, LLMs certainly make ML research faster. Maybe even 10x in some cases, as the author suggests.

But that’s just the parts of ML research that take place within your compute environment, namely experiments on model architecture, training strategy, UI/UX, etc. The algorithms and software.

Just because that part of research is progressively accelerated does not imply that we’re on a collision course with world-ending “superintelligence”. It just means that you’ll get to the best possible model of your data faster. And even when your data is the entire corpus of textual knowledge, there is a limit to the utility that provides.

It just means that software engineering, data analysis, and other computational tasks will be less of a bottleneck in the overall progress of the world (which, by the way, is great, and extremely valuable).

I don’t think it’s a stretch to say that we’ll have reached max LLM capability within a couple of years (what the author refers to as “super intelligence”). But it is a huge logical leap to say this:

> If we go through this feedback loop, I expect that the AI systems that come out the other side will be able to very quickly develop novel weapons and very easily overpower human civilization in a conflict.

First of all, the weapons necessary to overpower human civilization exist. They aren’t used as such due to geopolitics and humans’ basic survival instinct. Second, developing novel weapons requires physical tests, which are decidedly not accelerated by LLMs.

AI is a tool wielded by humans. If we’re wiped out by AI, it will be at the direction of a human. But we’ve made it pretty far with some pretty unstable humans in command of planet-killer weapons. I’m not overly concerned.

50401077.text:
Not really, no. Linux regards various ways of looking at the same on-disc filesystem format as distinct filesystem types: msdos, umsdos, vfat. Old Microsoft doco from the 1990s that is still lying around explains things in the way that they historically progressed rather than structurally, describing VFAT as an extension of FAT32.

The reality, certainly in respect of the headlined subject, is that the bitness of the FAT and the style of the root directory (fixed location or variable length) are the only meaningful variants. In 2026, no-one aims not to support long filenames on FAT, and EFI understands them natively. EFI copes with all three bitnesses. And it does the conventional thing of variable length root directory on 32-bit and fixed-length root directory on 16-bit and 12-bit.

FAT is a very poor filesystem format, and no, it's not a minimum filesystem format if one is writing one's own operating system. It's a lazy filesystem format, inasmuch as the cross-development tooling for it exists. But if one were writing a minimum filesystem for one's own operating system, one could start from much better places. FAT is not minimal by any reasonable definition even if one is not writing one's own operating system, and requires an awful lot of hoops to be jumped through that are only there because one is being compatible with the cross-development tooling, several decades of historical changes, and whatnot.

One could use the original UFS, for example. LEAN exists. Over 20 years ago, I invented HPFS2.

Handling thousands of git pushes per second implies thousands of issues, thousands of PRs, tens of thousands of comments, thousands of Actions runs, and dozens of releases. How's that part of their infra going to scale?

AIUI they’ve chosen as their target the host userspace pt_regs, i.e. the kernel structure that stores Firecracker’s register state. If they can find it and write to it, they can control the complete register state of Firecracker.

I assume they chose it as their target because Firecracker, like most Linux KVM userspace [0], maps guest memory into its own address space, giving an easy place to write gadgets.

My personal favorite thing to poke into pt_regs is an actual privileged (CPL0) context. [1] Returning from the kernel right back to a controlled kernel context is allowed by the CPU :)

[0] Until fairly recently this was mandatory. These days it’s possible to ask KVM to map something into the guest without having it in host userspace memory.

[1] Corrupt pt_regs so it executes user memory in kernel mode:

https://seclists.org/oss-sec/2015/q3/291

I think this may be my favorite of all exploits I’ve ever written. In fact, I often made a point of not writing interesting exploits for corruption bugs I found, but this one was too much fun to pass up.

I don't really follow the logic in the article at all:

The argument is that Unitree's assembly process is currently very manual because there is no incentive to automate, which is because labor cost isn't the bottleneck here, where in the US labor cost are much higher, therefore the US will have incentive to automate more. Those are reasonable so far, until you try to use that as a conclusion that this is why the West will win?

First of all, what does he think the other 92% of the cost of manufacturing is? A small portion of that is materials and electricity, but the biggest part of the remaining cost is assembly tooling/fixtures for the assembly line, and a fully automated assembly line is much, much more expensive compared to a semi-automated or manual production line.

In other words: it's not that Unitree couldn't build fully automated assembly lines if they wanted to, but spending tens of millions of dollars fully automated assembly line that takes up floor space and requires even more labor for manual maintenance for a product that is only being produced by the hundreds to thousands in quantity every month rather than millions simply does not make economic sense to begin with.

Second, why is he assuming that a fully automated assembly line will be cheaper to build in the US than in China, especially since he toured a factory with fully automated assembly lines at BYD in China immediately after? And sure, I would absolutely argue that American software engineering is more efficient than Chinese when looked at as a whole, but the cost of programming an assembly line is a minor portion of the cost compared to actually getting the assembly line fixtures and tooling built.

Third, his cost estimate is way off if he thinks you can get the same product manufactured in the US for only 50% more. From my own anecdotal experience, a more realistic cost for US manufacturing for pretty much anything is minimum 300% to 1000% more expensive if you are to make the in the US, and the lack of a mature parts supply chain in the US is honestly a bigger issue than worker wage.

I was reading through and thought "surely I missed a step here" in more than one place.

They mention in part 1 having a write primitive that can hit a 64 byte region, but never really explained how that worked. I'm guessing this was them being able to have checksum offload write TCP/UDP checksum values into the overhang region past the valid data. Maybe the memory map was set up that way, but obviously relies on getting really lucky with getting their page table in the next page after their packet.

Also it was never called out, but as far as I can tell their exploit should only be able to target the beginning of pages for reading/writing. In order to rug-pull the socket logic that reads the IP IHL field, the IP header content needs to be in a page mapped to the guest. The only useful way to use this attack is to have the region spill out of the guest page into whatever page comes next in the kernel's memory map. (Which also makes the mentioning of the skb linear header kind of confusing, since that would be in a completely unrelated kernel memory region, and just have the data pointers pointing into their data, which is what happens for zero-copy network drivers, which presumably was set up for the kvm network for them to retain guest control over the packet.)

50401970.text:
Reminds me of the extremely interesting paper https://arxiv.org/abs/1904.05234 Flash Boys 2.0

Basically when somebody makes a pricing error on a decentralized cryptocurrency exchange there's a mob of automated arbitrage bots that try to trade against it. Who wins and actually gets to make the trade is mainly determined by how high of a transaction fee your bot is willing to pay.

You can win instantly by offering to trade with a transaction fee so high it almost wipes out all but a cent or two of the entire arbitrage profits, because nobody else will pay a higher fee.

Instead what happens is bots offer the lowest possible fee, then immediately increase their fee as soon as they see a competing bot try to take the trade with a higher fee. This results in the bot offering the highest fee changing every several milliseconds as the fee quickly grows.

The way Ethereum mining works, this results in the winning bot being randomly selected from among the set of bots "bidding" up the transaction fee: blocks are mined at random intervals of iirc about 20 seconds, and whoever had the highest bid at the time the next block is mined wins. <20 seconds of bidding is short enough that even with the bidding, the transaction fee doesn't get bid up particularly high, and the winner makes out with a highly profitable arbitrage trade.

By giving up a guaranteed win and instead rolling the dice against other bots, transaction fees stay low and everyone has a higher expected profit. It's coordination that happens without any communication between the participants and quite possibly the participants didn't realize they were in effect cooperating when they added the high speed bidding behavior to their bots.

However horizontal scaling has advantages in that it's easier to scale up and down incrementally. It gives you more aggregate network bandwidth for accessing disaggregated data. Disaggregation allows for independent scaling of compute and storage. Losing a single machine has a marginal impact on the cluster, which can enable you to use cheaper spot resources.

Basically, it's often easier to operate a system designed around horizontal scaling if you need resiliency.

Peter makes some excellent points in TFA and it’s a fun read.

But the situation has moved on, moving even further beyond the assertions Peter makes about the utility of the black-box generative approach.

In particular, LLMs are telling us a lot about those low-probability, never before seen sentences — it’s called CALU, the creative aspects of language use.

LLMs exhibit CALU; as we know they will happily create such sentences. And inspecting the LLMs does provide insight:

“It does change the epistemic situation substantially. A working system can be inspected, perturbed, retrained, lesioned, and compared with other systems. Building is not understanding, but it gives understanding a strong foothold.

Explaining creative language use in LLMs would not, by itself, explain creative language use in humans. But the artificial case matters even if the mechanisms turn out to be substantially different. At a minimum, LLMs are an existence proof of one pathway by which open-ended, context-sensitive language can arise.”

For much more, see this substack by Chandra Sripada, a U of Michigan linguist:

https://chandrasripada.substack.com/p/ai-and-the-retreat-of-...

He is interviewed by Sean Carroll on his excellent Mindscape podcast:

> Some time ago, we were made aware of multiple attempts to exploit our permissive licensing to hijack our work, with a direct view to replacing the project and aggressively monetising Linux on Apple Silicon. In some extreme cases, in-development feature code was being lifted straight out of our personal forks and published without attribution or lazily rewritten with LLM assistance to obfuscate its origin. It's snake oil.

Landlords have an inherent trade off between holding out for a tenant who would pay a higher rent and not having the unit vacant in the meantime. Holding out for longer than that helps the other landlords at your expense. Meanwhile there are a large number of landlords, there is no way for the ones using a given system to force the others to do the same, and a significant percentage of them don't.

So if the system tells the landlords using it to do the thing that would increase rents if every landlord was using it, the "defectors" who don't use the system win out over anyone using it, which means using the system rather than defecting would cause you to lose money and everyone would have the incentive to defect.

Whereas if all the system is doing is suggesting the optimal point in the trade off between holding out for a higher paying tenant and renting the unit sooner, without assuming the other landlords are being required to use the same system, that's the same thing an individual landlord would do if they're not colluding.

The actual way landlords collude is through zoning boards, because then they have an enforcement mechanism, i.e. if someone is trying to defect by adding new units to alleviate the limited supply then the other landlords can sic the government on them, having passed the various laws against constructing those units there.

No, that is not how reasoning works. It is perfectly valid reasoning to begin by positing entities that we may not be possible to create, such as supersonic airplanes, coherent light, quantum computers, rockets that can reach escape velocity, black holes, or infinitely long lines that are perfectly straight and infinitely thin. Indeed, you might say that the ability to reason about the consequences of premises that we do not know to be true is the thing that distinguishes reasoning, as such, from simple parroting.

It could very well be the case that creating superintelligence is impossible. We won't know for sure unless it is achieved. Nevertheless, we can use reasoning from the hypothesis that it is possible to predict some of the effects that would ensue were it to be achieved. This allows us to easily dismiss the most profoundly stupid arguments, such as, 'Can you explain how exactly an AI would develop a novel planet-killing weapon without anyone noticing and pulling the plug?'

This reasoning, however valid it may be, is of course of much less interest should it turn out that we are reasoning about an impossible situation. Many arguments have been suggested on both sides of the issue, but the arguments for impossibility are extremely weak; most of them are conclusively dispatched in https://arxiv.org/pdf/1703.10987.

So far I've turned off automatic memory creation in every harness I've used. Claude Code sometimes creates some anyway, and I probably delete 95% of them. The memories it creates are almost always relevant only to the specific task that it is currently working on. If it's a task I'll need to do again, then yeah, maybe that's useful. But that isn't the case most of the time, so I delete them to avoid cluttering context.

So the main improvement to memories I'd like to see is better judgment on which ones to create.

The parts about "dreaming" make me think of how agent transcripts contain a ton of information, which I think is currently under-utilized. I'll repeat advice I've seen here a few times: ingest your own transcripts into duckdb (claude code will build that pipeline in about 10 minutes) and do some data analysis on them. Some ideas if you don't know where to start: look at tool call failures to see if you can prevent common ones, check out if you have large cache misses and what causes them, look at various efficiency metrics over time (tokens per $, lines of code per tokens, etc.) with main thread vs sub-agents, etc. I started with this sort of things, and ended up following some threads to interesting insights. For example, I found indications that I tended to make Opus 5.5 / Sol 6.1 divide their work into units that were too small. They have the capacity to work on more stuff at once than older models, and I wasn't really taking advantage of that.

The general premise of the rental market is that if rents are high, the profits from building new rental units will justify the construction costs and then new units will be added until the rents go down, i.e. until it stops being profitable to add more.

This actually works unless you inhibit the construction of new units. Naturally that's what we've been doing, which is why it isn't working. But the solution is to stop inhibiting the construction of new units.

Because the alternatives don't actually work. Unless you can build enough units to meet demand, there aren't enough units. Which means you either have high prices which suppress demand because people who can't afford them are forced out, or shortages because you're imposing some inadvisable price controls and then instead of being unable to get a unit because you can't afford the rent, you can't get a unit because they're all occupied and no one is adding more.

So much of my personal and anecdotally collected experience from others is essentially being locked out of knowledge and ideation because a "upper geek class" decided that they were not worthy of having their idea shared, specifically because that class thought they could make money from it, or because they were insular for some other in group reason. That’s not accurate. One leading hypothesis is that the experience of dreaming is a side effect of memory processing and consolidation[1]. Using the name of a side effect to describe the process that produces it is misleading, and at best it goes well beyond what’s actually known.

50403251.text:
Always cool to see this come up. I really like the idea of "encoding" the video as... x86 machine instructions!

The hairsplitting nerd in me can't help but point out that the claim in the Part 2 article that the problem of combining deltas is NP hard isn't true. In fact you can solve this optimally in O(n^3) time with DP: Let g(i, j) be the minimum number of bytes needed to encode input deltas i..j as a single (i.e., combined) output delta. Given g(i, j), computing g(i, j+1) takes constant time, so we can compute all of this function's values in O(n^2) total time. Now let f(i, j) be the minimum number of bytes needed to encode input deltas i..j using any sequence of output deltas (combined or not). Note that any such sequence must consist of some number (possibly zero) of optimally encoded output deltas followed by an optimally encoded output delta that itself ends with input delta j. IOW, it must be that f(i, j) is equal to f(i, k) + g(k+1, j) for some k, and there are at most n values of k that we need to try, so we can compute each value of f() in O(n); there are O(n^2) values to compute, so O(n^3) time overall. f(1, n) is then the minimum number of bytes needed to encode the entire list of input deltas, and standard backtracing through the DP matrix can be used to recover the actual sequence of output deltas.

50403324.text:
think of it as the split between a browser engine (renders and handles interactions with webpages) and a browser (provides the user interface and everything other than rendering the webpage, e.g. bookmarks, tabs, clipboard interaction, etc.)

similarly, a terminal conceptually consists of a terminal engine, which handles text rendering and interaction, and then a terminal which handles tabs, splits, sessions, etc.

now one key point is that you can get a terminal engine right according to a bunch of reasonably objective criteria, so it's a problem well worth solving once and for all. the terminal itself is a lot more subjective and idiosyncratic; different people want different things out of their terminals and the reason is very often that it fits the way they work, or they enjoy some particular features, and even the absence of other features. it is wonderful that libghostty can solve the part that everyone agrees needs to be objectively correct, and lets people concentrate on building the subjective part in the way they like best.
